Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Working Lands & Industry' — forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture, the resource economy that defines the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: geopolitical and war news with no resource-economy connection; consumer tech and gadget reviews; wildlife content with no agricultural or working-lands relevance; crime and judicial news unrelated to resource industries; financial market and stock ticker stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Trade-press journalism counts fully: equipment, markets, and operations coverage is a real fit, not a near-zero. A BC tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent working-lands journalism. BC/Cariboo forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture stories land here (mill closures, beetle kill, BCTS, Cariboo ranchers and water rights, local mine operations, Cariboo Cattlemen) — and so does outstanding national trade reporting with real operational or economic depth.
- 55-79: Solid resource-economy journalism anywhere in Canada or beyond — Western Producer or Northern Miner-style coverage of farm machinery, harvest technology, livestock and commodity markets, mining operations and exploration, AgTech and precision agriculture, silviculture, sawmills, drone survey work, mine automation, and labour/workforce stories in these industries. Most genuine trade journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Broader agriculture, forestry, or mining news with clear working-lands relevance but thin reporting — general farm economics, international resource-industry briefs, climate impacts on working lands.
- 15-29: Tangential mentions — a business, policy, or science story that touches forestry/agriculture/mining in passing, or Cariboo civic news unrelated to working lands.

items.title: [space.com] Researchers grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil using 30% compost
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Oregon State University researchers grew potatoes through their full life cycle in simulated lunar regolith after adding organic matter; a mixture containing 30% vermicompost produced yields comparable to those in terrestrial soil. The NASA-funded experiment took place in a greenhouse on Earth and used simulated material, not material collected on the moon, so it does not establish that crops can be grown on the lunar surface. The trial used five regolith simulants and the Modoc potato variety. Researchers plan to test 10 more potato varieties and are studying growth in larger pots; the first trial’s small pots produced small tubers.

items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The International Energy Agency says the energy disruption linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran is accelerating countries’ shift toward electrification. The agency said 25 countries had announced new electrification-related policies since February as governments seek more domestic energy sources. At the U.N. climate talks, COP31, host Türkiye is pressing to raise electricity’s share of global energy use from about 21% to 35% by 2035; draft negotiating text does not specify that the added power must come from renewables. The IEA also said buildings now use more energy for cooling than for heating, a shift it links to rising temperatures and demand for air conditioning. The agency expects solar and nuclear power to gain ground, but energy-security concerns could keep coal in use as backup, particularly in coal-rich Asian economies. It warned that inadequate electricity grids, charging infrastructure and supply capacity could slow electrification.

items.title: [leparisien.fr] Powerful El Niño nears December peak as droughts, fires threaten crops
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization says the powerful El Niño underway in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and likely persist through February 2027, disrupting rainfall and raising drought and flood risks worldwide. Sea-surface temperatures in the key Niño 3.4 region rose from 1.6°C above normal in June to 2.5°C above normal in August; forecasters project temperatures about 3.7°C above normal in October-December, exceeding the previous record of 2.6°C above normal. Recent impacts include drought and fires in Brazil, extensive forest fires in Indonesia, and a possible 21% to 25% decline in Ivory Coast cocoa output. Researchers attributed Indonesia’s July-October rainfall deficit largely to El Niño, while saying human-caused climate change made the atmospheric conditions about three times more likely and more intense. The United Nations Development Programme says acting now to limit the impacts would cost $36 billion, compared with $73 billion if action is delayed.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Alberta bill sets data-centre limits and well cleanup funds
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well. Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt. For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing.

items.title: [lethbridgeherald.com] B.C.'s first Conservative premier in nearly a century takes office
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Lorne Doerkson was sworn in Friday as British Columbia’s 38th premier, leading the province’s first Conservative government in almost a century after the party won 63 seats. His cabinet has 18 ministers and six ministers of state. He said it will focus on affordability, the economy, health care and public safety. The new government plans to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA), with a bill expected in spring 2027, and has promised to raise the personal income tax exemption from $13,216 to $32,000. Doerkson will not recall the legislature for a fall session. His cabinet is due to meet next week, when it may consider orders-in-council, including action on school resources on sexual orientation and gender identity.

items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The European Commission proposed on Nov. 18 an additional €45 billion loan for Ukraine in 2027, covering about two-thirds of a projected €70 billion funding gap. It would supplement the €90 billion EU loan already approved for 2026 and 2027; the new package allocates up to €25 billion for military needs and €20 billion for Ukraine’s state budget. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the funding was intended to strengthen Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Russia. Ukraine would repay the principal only after receiving Russian reparations. The EU would raise the money on capital markets, with its common budget guaranteeing the borrowing. Budget support would be conditional on Ukrainian reforms, including on the rule of law and corruption. The Commission also wants other international partners to cover the remaining €25 billion of Ukraine’s estimated needs. Approval faces resistance from Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia, which have signalled they do not want to join the financing. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pressed for all 27 EU members to share responsibility and linked the Ukraine financing to talks on the bloc’s next long-term budget; Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico called that approach “blackmail”. EU leaders are due to discuss the proposal at a Brussels summit on Nov. 26-27, and the budget guarantee requires unanimous member-state backing.

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

The readings point to about 0.3% growth for the eurozone in the fourth quarter, but suggest France’s economy is close to stalling. France’s economy contracted 0.1% in the third quarter, leaving it at risk of a technical recession if output falls again. S&P Global said French companies were holding back projects because of weak demand and uncertainty ahead of the April 2027 presidential election. The government is also struggling to pass a deficit-reduction budget. Persistent price pressures could strengthen calls for another European Central Bank rate increase in December, while higher borrowing costs are already weighing on activity. Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin, however, said he expects the French economy to grow in the fourth quarter.

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi condemned the attacks and called for them to stop. The agency has not publicly assigned responsibility for the strikes.

items.title: [physicsworld.com] Scientists propose supercritical fluids drove deep Mariana volcanic eruptions
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Researchers propose that supercritical water in magma could explain how volcanic deposits formed more than 6,000 meters down the Mariana Trench wall, building on the discovery of unusually deep pyroclastic rocks. At those pressures, water behaves neither like an ordinary liquid nor a gas and expands far less than steam. The team says this may have enabled magma to fragment without the force of a land eruption. The mechanism remains uncertain: researchers have not found the vents or directly observed an eruption. Rock samples contain “double breccia,” suggesting two closely spaced episodes of fracturing — one possibly linked to supercritical fluid and another to its conversion to steam at the seafloor. The team plans further analysis of the volcanic material and aims to explore farther along the plate boundary. Jason/Medea cannot descend below 6,500 meters, short of the Challenger Deep floor at about 11,000 meters.
